whenAndWhere: Berkshire, June 1981: a fenced ordnance factory in flat farmland outside Reading, on a road with no bus at that hour. The country is eighteen months into the cruise-missile decision and two months past Brixton.
inTheAir: NATO's 1979 decision brought cruise missiles to Greenham and Molesworth, and last summer's Trident order gave this factory a future rather than a wind-down.
Protect and Survive was published to be laughed at, and Thompson's reply to it has recruited more people this year than any speech.
Manchester declared a nuclear-free zone in November and dozens of councils have copied the wording, none of which stops a lorry on their roads.
Men are still dying on hunger strike in the Maze, and every argument about deliberately breaking the law this summer is had in that shadow.
contested: Some say arrestable actions frighten off the members the movement has only just gained; others answer that a membership card has never stopped a lorry.
Some say the American bases are the target because the missiles are American; others answer that the warheads are made here and leave through this gate.
exhausted: The CND symbol, twenty-three years old and printed on tea towels.
The mushroom cloud, which promises the end and asks for nothing.
The Hiroshima shadow on a wall, borrowed without its date.
The skeleton in a gas mask, dependable at every Easter march.

whoIsWatching.audience: A student teacher of twenty-six waits for a friend in a Reading bookshop and reads what is pinned by the till. She thinks it was all settled long ago somewhere she cannot reach, and she has never been arrested for anything. Being told exactly what it will cost her would keep her reading; being flattered as brave would not.
whoIsWatching.adversary: The Ministry police at the site, who pass copies to Special Branch and use the printed hour to close the approach road and turn a coach back before dawn.
